some more pictures-here's a regular rugelii, although notice how it's turning orange. In this case, it's due to mechanical damage:




Most likely, the culprit were exyra moths. Notice how undamaged traps are normal in color(yellowish-green):



One more shot:



Just to recap, here's a plant in Liberty Co, FL that also turned orange-ish due to mechanical damage:



A very happy cluster of S. flava var. rugelii, this appears to be 2 or 3 different clones:



Another shot:



Nice red throats:



and to get an idea of the habitat:



Really nice shapes:




And last but not least for the rugelii's, a color form, although this time, the color is genetic and not due to mechanical injury:


It had a nice red throat:


This was a pretty interesting plant:


A different clone, maybe this was S. flava var. ornata?


Couple more pics coming soon!

Missed your question KE: That white is definitely from S. leucophylla-the lids don't turn white as they age, and there was no manipulation of the image. Also, check out the ruffles in the lid of that plant and compare it to the "regular flavas" at that site.

we also saw a similar looking plant in another bog. There were definitely lots of mooreis around, and indeed, us blokes (busted a google search on that one) rolled pretty deep into the forest and encountered quite an array of plants.


Here are some more mooreis from the same site. This very first plant makes me think the red or orange/ornate forms at this site resulted from moorei parents or back-crossing with mooreis.



same exact plant, top view. Hard to tell from this angle that this is a moorei. If leucophylla can be back-crossed to the point that it looks "pure" why can't flava?



Us blokes ran into this beauty too:
